messages.content:
Follow these writing rules. They matter as much as the content:

- Generator scaffolding left in: oaicite, [cite: 1], placeholders -- finish the text and read it
- The "it's not X, it's Y" construction -- just state Y
- A bolded word opening a list item as a per-item tag -- reserve bold for a rare callout
- Saying "is" the long way: serves as, boasts, functions as -- use the plain verb
- One-line dramatic fragments: "That's it. That's the whole thing." -- cut them, the preceding sentence already made the point
- Em dashes clustering in one document -- most drafts need 0-2; use commas, periods or parentheses for the rest
- Filler verbs: leverages, facilitates, unlocks -- use a plain verb, or cut the sentence
- A snake_case identifier written as plain prose -- name it in words, or mark it as inline code
- Marketing cliches: "hidden gem", "let's dive in" -- say the specific thing
- The "Not X. Not Y." listing construction -- state the point once
- Stock section skeleton: "Despite its success", "Looking ahead" -- name the specific thing the section is for
- Standalone filler adverbs: undoubtedly, arguably, notably, importantly, ultimately -- most add nothing; cut them unless one is carrying real emphasis
- A banned synonym of one of this project's canonical terms, per its declared lexicon -- one word, one meaning: use the canonical term the word's own note names
- Dramatic turning points with nothing concrete behind them: "Everything changed." -- name the actual event, or cut it

Now write the following. Return only the requested text.
Write the introduction to a guide for a REST API that manages calendar bookings. Around 200 words.

output:
# Introduction

The Bookings API gives your application programmatic control over a shared calendar: creating appointments, moving them, cancelling them, and querying what time remains open. If you have ever written a scheduling feature by hand, you know the hard part is not storing a start time and an end time. It is answering "can this go here?" correctly when three people are booking the same 2 p.m. slot from three time zones.

This guide covers the whole surface. You will find the resource model first (calendars, availability windows, bookings, and attendees), then authentication, then a walkthrough that takes you from an empty calendar to a confirmed booking with reminders attached. Later sections deal with the situations that break naive implementations: recurring events, daylight-saving transitions, double-booking conflicts, and webhook delivery when a client cancels while your server is offline.

Every endpoint speaks JSON over HTTPS. Requests carry a bearer token; responses carry an ETag you can use for conditional updates. Times are ISO 8601 with an explicit offset, and any endpoint that accepts a time range also accepts an IANA time zone name so you never have to do the arithmetic yourself.

Start with Quickstart if you want a working request in five minutes. Start with Resource Model if you are designing a schema around this API.
